implementation_notes: The .NET mud form is a handful of assemblies that reference each other in both directions (which MSBuild only permits through project references and `InternalsVisibleTo`, so it shows up as an ever-growing reference list) plus a `Common`/`Utils` project that everything depends on and that in turn depends on several of them. Diagnosis is the reference graph, which the IDE shows directly. Consolidation is comparatively painful in C# because circular project references are a build error rather than a convention: the usual first move is to make the shared project depend on interfaces declared in a lower-level assembly, and to invert the specific cycle that hurts most.
idiom_name: a few projects referencing each other; shared static helper library
pitfalls: `InternalsVisibleTo` breaks the assembly boundary without making the dependency visible in the reference list.
A `Common` project is the most common mud generator in .NET codebases: it accumulates helpers that need types from every other project.
Reflection-based IoC configuration removes the compile-time cycle and replaces it with a runtime one, which is harder to see and harder to fix.
